items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: What’s Woody Allen like to collaborate with? ... we’ve always gotten along pretty well.

ctx.x: What’s Woody Allen like to collaborate with?

Well if I had to characterize it in a particular way I’d say knowledgeable, musically. He knows music. He picks the tunes. He’s open to suggestion and it’s easy to work with him, as opposed to some people who don’t know very much about the subject at all and may still give you a hard time. But the people who know that they don’t know about the subject, they’re okay to work with, they leave it to you. Woody is both. Woody leaves it to me and to the other people, I presume, the costumers and the set designers and…
When you’re doing a tune for a movie that’s not nearly as music-specific, and you have to do background things for certain scenes, how does that music evolve? Is it his suggestion of songs or is it—

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: the films I’ve done with Woody have been one way of writing

ctx.x: Great. Can you tell us about working in the modern day era these days, what it takes to keep working and maybe some of the film work you’ve done with Woody Allen and so forth? Has that been a pleasant experience? Something you like to do?

Well I found that film music writing demands just about everything I’ve ever known, not just one aspect or another aspect, but such a job requires just about everything I know, because I do my own orchestration. And the films I’ve done with Woody have been one way of writing, and I did a bunch of other things too. They’re all different, they all require a different approach, and they all require a cooperative way of creating the music, that is to say you have to be on the same wavelength as the director and the…
Oh yeah. You just did “Sugar Babies” not that long ago.
